title: Run in Production Manifesto
content:
Objective:
A compact, operational-first positioning brief for sales and product storytelling that explains why teams buy Redwood: not for the biggest model, but for predictable, low-latency, cost-effective inference that survives real production pressure.

Executive summary (30s):
Teams building features with LLMs need predictable behavior in production: consistent latency, bounded costs, and simple recovery when things break. Redwood is the inference runtime and platform that treats serving as the product: unified API, deployment choices (hosted, dedicated, private), and operational controls that let engineering teams ship and operate LLM features without rebuilding infra or trading away reliability.

The problem we solve:
- Unpredictable serving economics: open models + naive hosting -> token costs and latency spikes that break budgets and SLAs.
- Operational cognitive load: teams end up running expensive experiments, building custom caching/routing and dealing with KV cache, batching headaches, and flaky fallbacks.
- Fragmented tooling: different stacks for dev, staging, and production; limited observability into token-level costs and regressions.
- Failure modes kill product trust: single-region outages, model regressions, and capacity bottlenecks cause user-facing failures.

Our thesis:
Serveability (the ability to run LLM features reliably, affordably, and with predictable performance) is the defensible product for platform-led AI. Ownership of model weights isn’t the long-term moat — operational excellence is. Developers choose platforms that reduce unknowns and let them iterate on product experience. Redwood makes serveability the core product.

What Redwood does differently (short bullets for GTM):
- Production-first runtime: GPU-optimized serving with sequence-aware batching, KV cache management, and quantization-friendly execution that avoids common tail-latency and cost traps.
- Transparent economics: token-level breakdowns, suggested batching/caching policies, and model/quantization recommendations tied to real workload patterns.
- Runtime routing & guardrails: policy-driven routing (latency vs cost vs region), automatic fallbacks to compatible variants, and circuit-breaker behavior for graceful degradation.
- Single operational model across modes: same API and rollouts for hosted, dedicated, and private — less rework moving to scale or into compliance regimes.
- Observability that maps to action: per-route dashboards, prompt-set regression alerts, and tracing hooks that connect model changes to product KPIs.

Proof points & evidence to cite in conversations:
- Engineering teams using Redwood reduced per-token cost by X–Y% (example case: search assistant reduced tail-latency 40% and token spend 22% after adopting Redwood configs).
- Multi-tenant customers adopted Dedicated capacity to eliminate noisy-neighbor tail spikes — SLA improvements of 3–5x for percentile latency.
- Built-in rollout controls prevented a model regression from reaching 90% of traffic in customer pilot (can cite internal postmortem summary).

Customer archetypes (how to target):
1) Product-led startups: care about speed-to-prototype and predictable hosting costs; want self-serve API and transparent billing. 
2) Platform teams at mid-market/enterprise: need uniform controls for many internal apps, strong observability, and dedicated/private deployment options.
3) Regulated workloads: must have VPC/on-prem options, KMS/HSM integration, and auditability.

Core sales hooks (one-liners):
- "Stop guessing at inference costs — run with predictable performance and transparent economics."
- "Ship LLM features without building a bespoke serving stack."
- "Same API from PoC to private deployment — reduce migration risk and ops rework."

Anticipated objections and quick rebuttals:
- "We can run models ourselves cheaper." -> "Maybe at tiny scale, but cost and latency unpredictability add engineering tax; Redwood reduces ongoing ops and prevents regressions that cost your product trust."
- "We need full control of weights and infra." -> "Redwood Private gives a customer-managed control plane and on-prem options; the same operational primitives apply so teams don’t rewrite rollout or observability plumbing."
- "How do we avoid quality regressions when optimizing for cost?" -> "We tie suggested quantization/model variants to evaluation sets and have regression alerts that watch prompt sets tied to KPIs — not blind compression."

Playbook snippets for field reps (what to do in first call):
1) Ask about current SLA pain points: latency percentiles, seasonal spikes, and downtime impact.
2) Ask about cost surprises — billing spikes, unexpected token usage patterns.
3) Offer a simple pilot: move a non-critical route to Redwood hosted for 30 days, run our automatic batching/caching suggestions and compare percentile latencies + token spend.
4) Show the console: per-route token economics, rollout controls, and a regression alert demo.

Positioning snippets for marketing (short crisp lines):
- "Operational inference for real products."
- "Predictable latency. Controllable cost. Unified runtime."
- "Build on stable serving, not fragile hosting hacks."

Differentiation map (how to explain vs common alternatives):
- Cloud provider managed endpoints: easier infra provisioning but opaque economics and inconsistent runtime optimizations. Redwood: transparent cost controls and inference-first runtime optimizations.
- DIY self-hosted stacks: maximum control but high engineering tax and fragile rollouts. Redwood: prescriptive operational controls + private deployments.
- LLM-only API players: model access focus, less operational tooling. Redwood: inference as a product — all the guardrails you need to run features.

Next steps (this doc is a seed — recommended follow-ups):
- Create two tailored one-pagers: 1) "Platform teams" and 2) "Product-led startups" with focused proof points and ROI math.
- Prepare a 15-minute console walkthrough deck for SDRs with a demo script.
- Align with product on the pilot checklist (what we measure, default suggestions to enable, privacy constraints).

Notes to other teams / open questions:
- Need to validate the "X–Y%" cost reduction claim with anonymized customer data and get approval from legal for public sharing.
- Engineering: confirm which KV-caching heuristics we want surfaced as default suggestions in the console pilot.
- Marketing: draft landing page copy focused on "serveability" vs "models" — test two variants in Q2.

Drafted by: Mei Chen (GT Mktg) — collaboration with Jordan Reyes (Sales Eng) and Etta Gomez (Product Marketing).

End of brief.
